paragraphs.heading: Our star
paragraphs.text: The Sun is the star at the centre of the Solar System. It is a giant ball of hot plasma, made to glow by nuclear fusion reactions deep in its core. From its surface it gives off that energy mainly as visible light and infrared, with 10% coming out as ultraviolet. Life on Earth runs mainly on the energy it sends us.

paragraphs.heading: Size and distance
paragraphs.text: On average the Sun is about 1.496×10⁸ kilometres from Earth, a distance light covers in about 8 minutes. That distance was used to set a unit of length, the astronomical unit (au). The Sun is the biggest and heaviest thing in the Solar System: about 1,391,400 km across, roughly 109 times Earth's width. Its mass is around 330,000 times Earth's, about 99.86% of all the mass in the Solar System. Its surface layer, the photosphere, is mostly hydrogen (~73%) and helium (~25%), with small amounts of heavier elements such as oxygen, carbon, neon and iron.

paragraphs.heading: How it was born
paragraphs.text: The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago, when matter inside part of a large molecular cloud collapsed under its own gravity. Most of that matter piled up in the middle, while the rest spread into a flat, circling disk that became the Solar System. The central mass grew so hot and dense that fusion eventually switched on in its core.

paragraphs.heading: What kind of star
paragraphs.text: Every second, the core fuses about 600 billion kilograms of hydrogen into helium and turns four billion kilograms of matter into energy. Astronomers class the Sun as a G2V star, a G-type main-sequence star. The 2 means its surface temperature falls in the second range of the G class. With an absolute magnitude of +4.83, it is thought to outshine roughly 85% of the Milky Way's stars, most of which are red dwarfs.

paragraphs.heading: How it will end
paragraphs.text: In about four to seven billion years, hydrogen fusion in the core will fade until the Sun can no longer hold its balance. The core will then grow much denser and hotter, pushing the outer layers outward until the Sun becomes a red giant. Models suggest it will next throw off those outer layers and become a white dwarf, a dense, cooling star that no longer fuses anything but still glows with stored heat, perhaps for trillions of years. After that, it is expected to end as a black dwarf, extremely dense and giving off almost no energy.

paragraphs.heading: Almost perfectly round
paragraphs.text: One measure of the Sun's shape, its oblateness, is very hard to pin down, and because the air distorts the view it has to be measured from satellites. When the Solar Dynamics Observatory and the Picard satellite measured it precisely, the result was smaller than anyone expected: 8.2×10⁻⁶, which is 8 parts per million. That makes the Sun the closest thing to a perfect sphere of any natural object ever observed. Yet it does not spin as one solid piece. Measured against the stars, its equator turns once in about 25.6 days, while its poles take about 33.5 days.
